column4: Suppose you had $100 in a savings account and the interest rate was 2% per year. After 5 years, how much do you think you would have in the account if you left the money to grow?
column5: You put $100 in a savings account earning 2% interest per year. After 5 years, will you have: more than $102, exactly $102, or less than $102?
column6:
A) More than $102
B) Exactly $102
C) Less than $102
D) Do not know
column9: Your money earns interest, then that interest earns MORE interest (compound interest). After 5 years at 2%, you'd have about $110. This is how savings grow over time - money makes money!
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Imagine that the interest rate on your savings account was 1% per year and inflation was 2% per year. After 1 year, how much would you be able to buy with the money in this account?
column5: Your savings earn 1% interest, but prices rise 2% per year. After 1 year, can you buy MORE, the SAME, or LESS stuff with your savings?
column6:
A) More than today
B) Exactly the same
C) Less than today
D) Do not know
column9: If prices rise faster than your savings grow, you can buy LESS even though you have more dollars. This is why inflation matters - your money loses 'buying power' if it's not keeping up.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Please tell me whether this statement is true or false: Buying a single company's stock usually provides a safer return than a stock mutual fund.
column5: Is it SAFER to own stock in ONE company or to own a fund with stocks from MANY companies?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: FALSE - a mutual fund is safer. If you own just one company and it fails, you lose everything. A fund owns hundreds of stocks, so one company failing barely hurts you. Don't put all eggs in one basket!
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: If interest rates rise, what will typically happen to bond prices?
column5: When interest rates GO UP, what happens to the price of bonds you already own?
column6:
A) They will rise
B) They will fall
C) They will stay the same
D) There is no relationship
E) Do not know
column9: Bond prices FALL. When new bonds offer higher interest, your old bond with a lower rate is worth less. It's like trying to sell an old phone when better models come out.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: A 15-year mortgage typically requires higher monthly payments than a 30-year mortgage, but the total interest paid over the life of the loan will be less. True or false?
column5: A 15-year mortgage has HIGHER monthly payments but LOWER total interest than a 30-year mortgage. True or false?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. Paying faster means bigger monthly bills but WAY less interest overall. A 30-year mortgage might cost you twice as much in total interest! Time = money with loans.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: High inflation means that the cost of living is increasing rapidly. True or false?
column5: Does 'high inflation' mean that everyday things like food and rent are getting more expensive quickly?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. Inflation = rising prices. High inflation means your grocery bill, rent, and gas prices are climbing fast. Understanding this helps you plan your budget and savings.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: If someone offers you the chance to make a lot of money, it is likely that there is also a chance that you will lose a lot of money. True or false?
column5: If someone promises you can make BIG money, is there usually also a big chance of LOSING money?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. High reward = high risk. There's no free lunch in investing. If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is. Scammers love to promise 'guaranteed' high returns.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: You lend $25 to a friend one evening and he gives you $25 back the next day. How much interest has he paid on this loan?
column5: You lend a friend $25 tonight and they pay you back $25 tomorrow. How much interest did you earn?
column6:
A) $25
B) $0
C) Do not know
column9: ZERO. Interest is the EXTRA money paid for borrowing. If they paid back the same amount, there's no interest. Interest is like a rental fee for using someone else's money.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Imagine that five friends are given a gift of $1,000. If the friends have to share the money equally, how much does each one get?
column5: Five friends split $1,000 equally. How much does each person get?
column6:
A) $100
B) $150
C) $200
D) $250
E) Do not know
column9: $1,000 ÷ 5 = $200 each. Basic division is essential for budgeting - splitting bills, calculating tips, dividing expenses among roommates.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: An investment with a high return is likely to be high risk. True or false?
column5: Do investments that promise HIGH returns usually come with HIGH risk?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. This is the golden rule of investing. Stocks return more than savings accounts because they're riskier. Anyone promising high returns with no risk is lying or scamming.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Suppose you put $100 into a no-fee savings account with a guaranteed interest rate of 2% per year. You don't make any further payments into this account and you don't withdraw any money. How much would be in the account at the end of the first year, once the interest payment is made?
column5: You put $100 in savings at 2% annual interest. After one year, how much do you have?
column6:
A) $52
B) $102
C) $128
D) $152
E) Do not know
column9: $102. Simple: $100 × 2% = $2 interest. Total = $102. This is year one - in future years, you'd earn interest on $102, then on that new total, and so on (compound growth).
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: And how much would be in the account at the end of five years? Would it be more than $110, exactly $110, or less than $110?
column5: After 5 years at 2% interest starting with $100, will you have: more than $110, exactly $110, or less than $110?
column6:
A) More than $110
B) Exactly $110
C) Less than $110
D) Do not know
column9: MORE than $110. With compound interest, you earn 'interest on interest.' Each year's balance is bigger, so you earn more. After 5 years at 2%, you'd have about $110.41. Over decades, this adds up BIG.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Suppose you have $100 in a savings account earning 2% interest a year. After five years, how much would you have?
column5: $100 at 2% interest for 5 years. Will you end up with: more than $110, exactly $110, less than $110, or exactly $102?
column6:
A) More than $110
B) Exactly $110
C) Less than $110
D) Exactly $102
column9: MORE than $110. Compound interest means your interest earns interest. It's not just 5 × $2 = $10. The real amount is about $110.41. This 'snowball effect' is how wealth builds over time.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Which of the following best describes what the stock market does?
column5: What does the stock market DO?
column6:
A) Results in a gain in wealth for investors
B) Creates liquidity by__(cut for space)__
C) Brings people who want to buy stocks together with those who want to sell stocks
D) Do not know
column7: C) Brings people who want to buy stocks together with those who want to sell stocks
column9: The stock market is a MARKETPLACE - it connects buyers and sellers. It doesn't guarantee profits or predict the future. Think of it like eBay for company ownership.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: If a young person with a long-term investment horizon has money to invest, which will typically produce the best returns?
column5: For a young person investing for 30+ years, which typically gives the BEST returns: savings account, bonds, or stocks?
column6:
A) Savings account
B) Government bonds
C) Stocks
D) Do not know
column9: STOCKS, typically. Over long periods (30+ years), stocks have historically returned about 10% per year vs. 5% for bonds vs. 1-2% for savings. The longer your time horizon, the more you can ride out short-term drops.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Lyle has a good job and earns enough to pay his bills comfortably each month. In terms of his emergency savings, how much should he have set aside?
column5: How much emergency savings should someone have set aside?
column6:
A) $200 or so
B) Money equal to his share of one month's rent/mortgage
C) The equivalent of three or more months of living expenses
D) Do not know
column7: C) The equivalent of three or more months of living expenses
column9: 3+ MONTHS of expenses. If you lose your job or have an emergency, you need time to recover. $200 won't cover much. Most experts say 3-6 months of rent, food, and bills.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: A successful effort to lower inflation would likely be accompanied by which of the following?
column5: If the government successfully LOWERS inflation, what usually happens to prices?
column6:
A) A decrease in the general level of prices
B) A slower increase in prices
C) An increase in employment
D) Do not know
column7: B) A slower increase in prices
column9: Prices SLOW DOWN, they don't usually DROP. 'Low inflation' means prices still rise, just more slowly. Going from 8% to 2% inflation means prices grow slower, not that things get cheaper.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Inflation can cause difficulty in many ways. Which group would have the greatest problem during periods of high inflation?
column5: Who is HURT MOST by high inflation?
column6:
A) Young couples with no children who both work
B) Older, working couples saving for retirement
C) Retirees living on a fixed income
D) Do not know
column7: C) Retirees living on a fixed income
column9: RETIREES on fixed income. If your pension pays $2,000/month forever but prices double, you can only buy half as much. Workers can ask for raises; retirees often can't increase their income.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: A family member tells Wendy that her hourly wage will be cut 10% if she stays at her current job. In addition, her work hours would also be cut 10%. What best describes how her paycheck would change?
column5: If both your hourly pay AND your hours are cut by 10%, does your total pay drop by: less than 20%, exactly 20%, or more than 20%?
column6:
A) It would decrease by less than 20%
B) It would decrease by 20%
C) It would decrease by more than 20%
D) Do not know
column7: A) It would decrease by less than 20%
column9: LESS than 20%. If you made $100, a 10% pay cut = $90. Then 10% fewer hours on $90 = $81. You lost $19 (19%), not $20. When you cut BOTH factors, the cuts overlap slightly.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Which of the following best describes the PRIMARY function of health insurance?
column5: What is the MAIN purpose of health insurance?
column6:
A) Protect against the possibility of large unexpected medical bills
B) Cover the cost of routine health care expenses
C) Pay for elective medical procedures
D) Do not know
column7: A) Protect against the possibility of large unexpected medical bills
column9: Protection from BIG bills. Insurance isn't really for small costs - it's for the $50,000 surgery or $100,000 hospital stay that would bankrupt most people. It protects against catastrophic costs.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: What does a home insurance deductible represent?
column5: What is a 'deductible' in home insurance?
column6:
A) Amount you pay before insurance covers damages
B) Monthly premium for coverage
C) Maximum amount insurance will pay
D) Do not know
column7: A) Amount you pay before insurance covers damages
column9: YOUR share first. If you have a $1,000 deductible and $5,000 in damage, you pay the first $1,000, then insurance covers the rest ($4,000). Higher deductibles = lower premiums, but more out-of-pocket when claims happen.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Jayden is shopping for an auto loan. Which of the following can he likely negotiate with the lender?
column5: When getting a car loan, what can you usually NEGOTIATE with the lender?
column6:
A) The interest rate
B) The required down payment
C) Both
D) Neither
E) Do not know
column9: BOTH are negotiable. Banks want your business. You can often get a lower rate or smaller down payment by shopping around or having good credit. Never accept the first offer without asking!
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Considering the strategy of allocating income, what is the PRIMARY advantage to your household of making a budget?
column5: What is the MAIN benefit of making a budget for your household?
column6:
A) Ensures funds are available for bill paying and saving
B) Reduces your taxes
C) Increases rate of return on your investments
D) Do not know
column7: A) Ensures funds are available for bill paying and saving
column9: Knowing where your money goes. A budget helps you make sure rent gets paid before fun spending, and that you save something each month. It's a plan so you don't run out before payday.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Which of the following statements regarding credit reports is FALSE?
column5: Which statement about credit reports is WRONG?
column6:
A) Credit reports are used by employers to screen job applicants
B) A credit report includes an assessment of your worthiness to receive credit
C) Your credit report is provided by a single source
D) Do not know
column7: C) Your credit report is provided by a single source
column9: FALSE: There are THREE credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), not one. They may have different info. Check all three annually at annualcreditreport.com - it's free and catches errors.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: When an investor spreads money among different assets, the risk of losing money usually:
column5: When you spread your investments across different types (stocks, bonds, real estate), does your risk of losing money go UP, DOWN, or STAY THE SAME?
column6:
A) Increases
B) Decreases
C) Stays the same
D) Do not know
column9: DECREASES. Different investments don't all crash at once. When stocks drop, bonds might rise. Spreading out reduces the chance of losing everything at the same time.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: If interest rates go up, what will typically happen to bond prices? Will they rise, fall, stay the same, or is there no relationship?
column5: When interest rates RISE, do bond prices go UP, DOWN, or STAY THE SAME?
column6:
A) Rise
B) Fall
C) Stay the same
D) No relationship
E) Do not know
column9: They FALL. Old bonds paying low interest are worth less when new bonds pay more. This is called 'interest rate risk.' Bond funds lost money in 2022 when rates rose sharply.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Considering a long time period (e.g., 10-20 years), which asset normally gives the highest return?
column5: Over 10-20 years, which typically gives the HIGHEST return: savings accounts, bonds, or stocks?
column6:
A) Savings accounts
B) Bonds
C) Stocks
D) Do not know
column9: STOCKS. Historically, stocks return ~10%/year, bonds ~5%, savings ~2%. Over 20 years, $10,000 becomes ~$67,000 in stocks vs. ~$27,000 in bonds. Time smooths out the bumps.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: At what age can you receive FULL Social Security retirement benefits?
column5: At what age can you get your FULL Social Security retirement benefit (for people born 1960 or later)?
column6:
A) 62
B) 65
C) 67
D) 70
E) Do not know
column9: Age 67 (for those born 1960+). You CAN claim at 62, but you get about 30% less. Waiting until 70 gives you 24% more. Knowing this helps you plan when to retire.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Medicare is the federal health insurance program for people:
column5: Who does Medicare cover?
column6:
A) Below a certain income level
B) Age 65 and older
C) Unemployed
D) All of the above
E) Do not know
column9: People 65+ (and some disabled). Medicare is NOT based on income - that's Medicaid. Everyone becomes eligible at 65. Important: Medicare doesn't cover everything, especially long-term care.
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Which of the following statements about annuities is TRUE?
column5: What does an annuity do?
column6:
A) An annuity provides income in retirement that one cannot outlive
B) An annuity lets you invest in stocks without risk
C) An annuity is guaranteed by the FDIC
D) Do not know
column7: A) An annuity provides income in retirement that one cannot outlive
column9: Lifetime income you can't outlive. An annuity is like buying a personal pension - you give an insurance company money, and they pay you monthly for life. Protects against living 'too long.'
column11: Item bank with original and simplified wording, answer options, and answer key.

column4: Out of 1,000 people in a small town 500 are members of a choir. Out of these 500 members in the choir 100 are men. Out of the 500 inhabitants that are not in the choir 300 are men. What is the probability that a randomly drawn man is a member of the choir? Please indicate the probability in percent.
column5: In a town of 1,000 people: 500 are in a choir (100 men, 400 women), and 500 are NOT in the choir (300 men, 200 women). If you pick a random MAN from the town, what's the chance he's in the choir?
column6:
A) 12.5%
B) 15%
C) 25%
D) 35%
E) Do not know
column9: Count all the men: 100 + 300 = 400 men. How many are in the choir? 100. So 100 out of 400 = 25%. This skill helps you understand questions like 'Of all the people with this symptom, how many actually have the disease?'
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Imagine we are throwing a five-sided die 50 times. On average, out of these 50 throws how many times would this five-sided die show an odd number (1, 3 or 5)?
column5: A special die has 5 sides numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Three of those numbers are odd (1, 3, 5). If you roll this die 50 times, about how many times will you get an odd number?
column6:
A) 24
B) 25
C) 30
D) 35
E) Do not know
column9: 3 out of 5 sides are odd. So you expect odd numbers 3/5 of the time. 3/5 × 50 = 30 times. It's like saying: if a medicine works for 60% of people, out of 100 patients, about 60 will get better.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Imagine we are throwing a loaded die (6 sides). The probability that the die shows a 6 is twice as high as the probability of each of the other numbers. On average, out of these 70 throws, how many times would the die show the number 6?
column5: A trick die is weighted so rolling a 6 is TWICE as likely as rolling any other number. If you roll it 70 times, about how many 6s will you get?
column6:
A) 15
B) 16
C) 20
D) 24
E) Do not know
column9: Think of 7 equal 'chances': numbers 1-5 each get 1 chance, but 6 gets 2 chances. So 6 appears 2 out of 7 times. 2/7 × 70 = 20. This helps understand when some outcomes are more likely than others, like certain risk factors.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: In a forest 20% of mushrooms are red, 50% brown and 30% white. A red mushroom is poisonous with a probability of 20%. A mushroom that is not red is poisonous with a probability of 5%. What is the probability that a poisonous mushroom in the forest is red?
column5: In a forest: 20% of mushrooms are red, the rest are other colors. Red mushrooms: 20% are poisonous. Non-red mushrooms: only 5% are poisonous. If you find a POISONOUS mushroom, what's the chance it's red?
column6:
A) 25%
B) 40%
C) 50%
D) 60%
E) Do not know
column9: Imagine 100 mushrooms: 20 red (4 poisonous), 80 not red (4 poisonous). Total poisonous = 8. Of those 8, how many are red? 4. So 4/8 = 50%. This is crucial for medical tests: 'If you test positive, what's the real chance you're sick?'
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Imagine that we flip a fair coin 1,000 times. What is your best guess about how many times the coin would come up heads in 1,000 flips?
column5: If you flip a normal coin 1,000 times, about how many times will it land on heads?
column6:
A) 400
B) 495
C) 500
D) 505
E) Do not know
column9: A fair coin has a 50-50 chance. Half of 1,000 = 500. This basic idea is the foundation of all probability. When someone says '50% chance,' they mean about half the time.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: In the BIG BUCKS LOTTERY, the chance of winning a $10 prize is 1%. What is your best guess about how many people would win a $10 prize if 1,000 people each buy a single ticket?
column5: A lottery has a 1% chance of winning. If 1,000 people each buy one ticket, about how many winners will there be?
column6:
A) 5
B) 8
C) 10
D) 12
E) Do not know
column9: 1% means 1 out of every 100. So out of 1,000 people, that's 10 winners. This helps you understand real numbers: 'If a side effect happens to 2% of patients, that's 20 people out of 1,000.'
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: In the ACME PUBLISHING SWEEPSTAKES, the chance of winning a car is 1 in 1,000. What percent of tickets for ACME PUBLISHING SWEEPSTAKES win a car?
column5: If your chance of winning is 1 in 1,000, what is that as a percentage?
column6:
A) 0%
B) 0.1%
C) 0.2%
D) 10.1%
E) Do not know
column9: 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001 = 0.1%. This is converting between different ways of showing the same risk. Whether someone says '1 in 1,000' or '0.1%,' it means the same thing.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which of the following numbers represents the biggest risk of getting a disease?
column5: Which is the BIGGEST risk: 1 in 10, 1 in 100, or 1 in 1,000?
column6:
A) 1 in 100
B) 1 in 1,000
C) 1 in 10
D) Do not know
column9: The smaller the second number, the higher the risk. 1 in 10 = 10%. 1 in 100 = 1%. 1 in 1,000 = 0.1%. Would you rather be 1 unlucky person out of 10 or out of 1,000? Being 1 in 10 is much more likely.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which of the following numbers represents the biggest risk of getting a disease?
column5: Which percentage is the highest risk: 1%, 5%, or 10%?
column6:
A) 1%
B) 10%
C) 5%
D) Do not know
column9: Simply: which is largest? 10% > 5% > 1%. While this seems easy, many people get confused when risks are shown in different formats or with distracting context.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: If the chance of getting a disease is 10%, how many people would be expected to get the disease out of 100?
column5: If 10% of people get sick, how many is that out of 100 people?
column6:
A) 5
B) 8
C) 10
D) 12
E) Do not know
column9: 10% of 100 = 10. 'Percent' literally means 'per hundred.' So 10 percent of 100 is just 10. This turns abstract percentages into real numbers you can picture.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: If the chance of getting a disease is 10%, how many people would be expected to get the disease out of 1,000?
column5: If 10% of people get sick, how many is that out of 1,000 people?
column6:
A) 80
B) 95
C) 100
D) 105
E) Do not know
column9: 10% of 1,000 = 100. If 10 out of 100 get sick, then 100 out of 1,000 get sick (just multiply by 10). This helps you understand how risks affect larger populations.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: If the chance of getting a disease is 20 out of 100, this would be the same as having a ___% chance of getting the disease.
column5: 20 out of 100 equals what percent?
column6:
A) 10%
B) 20%
C) 30%
D) 40%
E) Do not know
column9: 'Per cent' means 'per hundred.' So 20 out of 100 = 20%. Being able to convert between formats helps you compare risks that are presented differently.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: There's a 50/50 chance that Malik's car will need engine repairs within the next six months which would cost $1,000. At the same time there is a 10% chance that he will need to replace the air conditioning unit in his house, which would cost $4,000. Which poses the greater financial risk for Malik?
column5: Malik has two possible expenses: Car repair - 50% chance, costs $1,000. AC replacement - 10% chance, costs $4,000. Which one should he worry about MORE financially?
column6:
A) The car engine repairs
B) The air conditioning replacement
C) Both pose the same financial risk
D) Do not know
column9: Multiply probability × cost. Car: 50% × $1,000 = $500 'expected cost.' AC: 10% × $4,000 = $400. The car costs less if it breaks, but it's much more likely to happen, making it the bigger financial risk overall.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which of the following indicates the highest probability of getting a particular disease?
column5: Which shows the HIGHEST chance of getting sick: '1 in 20 chance,' '2% probability,' or 'small likelihood'?
column6:
A) 1 in 20 chance
B) 2% probability
C) There is a small likelihood
D) Do not know
column9: Convert to same format: 1 in 20 = 5%. 2% = 2%. 'Small likelihood' = vague. So 5% > 2% > 'small.' Always convert to the same format (percentages) before comparing risks.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Consider a couple that has two children and are thinking about having a third child. The doctor tells them that boys and girls are equally likely to be born. What are the chances that the next child will be a girl?
column5: A couple already has two children. For their third child, what's the chance it will be a girl? (Boys and girls are equally likely.)
column6:
A) It depends on whether the first two children are boys or girls
B) 50%
C) 25%
D) Do not know
column9: Each birth is independent - what happened before doesn't change what happens next. It's always 50/50. This corrects the 'gambler's fallacy' - thinking past coin flips affect future ones.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: A friend recommends that you invest in a particular technology company. The expected return is 25% in the first year. Which of the following statements is true?
column5: Someone tells you an investment could return 25% in one year. What does this tell you about the risk?
column6:
A) The investment is likely to be very risky
B) The investment is likely no riskier than investing in multiple technology companies
C) Nothing can be inferred about the risk of the investment
D) Do not know
column7: A) The investment is likely to be very risky
column9: Higher expected returns = higher risk. The stock market averages about 10% per year. A 25% promise means high risk. There's no free lunch in investing - if it sounds too good, the risk is probably huge.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Buying a single company's stock usually provides a safer return than a stock mutual fund. True or false?
column5: Is owning stock in ONE company safer than owning a fund with MANY different company stocks?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: FALSE. A mutual fund owns many stocks, so if one company fails, you don't lose everything. With one stock, all your eggs are in one basket. Spreading out = less risk.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: When an investor spreads money among different assets, does the risk of losing money usually increase, decrease, or stay the same?
column5: If you spread your money across different types of investments, does your risk of losing money go UP, DOWN, or STAY THE SAME?
column6:
A) Increase
B) Decrease
C) Stay the same
D) Do not know
column9: DECREASE. Different investments don't all go up or down together. When stocks fall, bonds might rise. Spreading out smooths your overall results. Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: If someone offers you the chance to make a lot of money, it is likely that there is also a chance that you will lose a lot of money. True or false?
column5: If an opportunity promises BIG profits, does it also usually come with BIG risks of losing money?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. High reward = high risk. This is true for investments, business ventures, everything financial. If someone promises high returns with no risk, it's likely a scam.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: True or false: It is less likely that you will lose all of your money if you save it in more than one place.
column5: Are you SAFER keeping your savings in SEVERAL places instead of just ONE place?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. If you keep all savings in one bank and it fails, you lose everything. Spread across multiple places, and one failure doesn't wipe you out. Classic 'eggs in baskets' wisdom.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: If interest rates rise, what will typically happen to bond prices?
column5: When interest rates GO UP, what happens to the prices of existing bonds?
column6:
A) They will rise
B) They will fall
C) They will stay the same
D) There is no relationship between bond prices and the interest rate
E) Do not know
column9: They FALL. When new bonds offer higher rates, your old bond with a lower rate becomes less attractive. Like selling a used car when better new models come out - your old one is worth less.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which of the following insurance policies is most likely to protect you if you cause an accident that injures someone?
column5: Which insurance covers you if YOU cause an accident that hurts someone else?
column6:
A) Health insurance
B) Homeowner's or renter's insurance
C) Auto insurance liability coverage
D) Do not know
column9: Auto liability coverage. 'Liability' means covering damage YOU cause to OTHERS. Health insurance covers your own medical bills. Knowing which insurance covers what helps you avoid gaps in protection.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: True or false: If you have employer-provided health insurance, you generally cannot be charged more because of a pre-existing health condition.

column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE - they cannot charge more. Under US law (ACA), employer group plans can't charge more or deny coverage for pre-existing conditions. Knowing insurance rules helps you make smart job and coverage decisions.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Suppose you have the choice between a sure payment of $50 or a lottery where you have a 50% chance of winning $100 and a 50% chance of winning nothing. Which option has the higher expected value?
column5: Which is worth more on average: A guaranteed $50 OR a 50-50 chance at $100 or nothing?
column6:
A) The sure payment of $50
B) The lottery
C) Both have the same expected value
D) Do not know
column7: C) Both have the same expected value
column8: Expected Value - Lottery vs. Certain Outcome
column9: SAME value. Lottery: 50% × $100 + 50% × $0 = $50 on average. Sure thing = $50. Mathematically equal. Your choice depends on how you feel about risk - neither is 'wrong.'
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: You have two investment options. Investment A has a 60% chance of gaining $1,000 and a 40% chance of losing $500. Investment B has a guaranteed return of $400. Which investment has the higher expected value?
column5: Which is worth more on average? Option A: 60% chance to win $1,000, 40% chance to lose $500. Option B: Guaranteed $400.
column6:
A) Investment A
B) Investment B
C) Both have the same expected value
D) Do not know
column7: C) Both have the same expected value
column9: SAME value. A: (60% × $1,000) + (40% × -$500) = $600 - $200 = $400. B: $400. Both average $400. The difference is A has uncertainty, B is certain. Choose based on your comfort with risk.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which of the following types of investment would best protect the purchasing power of a family's savings in the event of a sudden increase in inflation?
column5: If prices suddenly shoot up (inflation), which protects your money best: a fixed-rate bond, a bank CD, or a house with a fixed-rate mortgage?
column6:
A) A 10-year bond paying a fixed rate of interest
B) A certificate of deposit at a bank
C) A 25-year home mortgage at a fixed rate
D) A house financed with a fixed-rate mortgage
E) Do not know
column7: D) A house financed with a fixed-rate mortgage
column9: The HOUSE. Real assets (like houses) typically rise with inflation, while your fixed mortgage payment stays the same. Bonds and CDs pay fixed amounts that buy less when prices rise. You win when your asset grows but your debt doesn't.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: Which type of risk can be reduced through diversification?
column5: Which type of risk can you reduce by spreading your investments: the risk from ONE company's problems, or the risk from the WHOLE market crashing?
column6:
A) Market risk (systematic risk)
B) Company-specific risk (unsystematic risk)
C) Both types of risk equally
D) Neither type of risk
E) Do not know
column9: Company-specific risk. If one company has problems, owning many stocks protects you. But market-wide events (recessions, wars) affect everything - you can't diversify away from those. That's why even diversified portfolios drop in crashes.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: True or false: Stocks are generally riskier than bonds.
column5: Are stocks generally RISKIER than bonds?
column6:
A) True
B) False
C) Do not know
column9: TRUE. Stocks = ownership, prices swing widely. Bonds = loans, more stable payments. Stocks offer higher long-term returns but with more ups and downs. Young investors often hold more stocks; retirees shift to bonds.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test for the disease is 99% accurate (it correctly identifies 99% of people who have the disease and 99% of people who don't have it). If a person tests positive, what is the approximate probability they actually have the disease?
column5: A rare disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test is 99% accurate. If you TEST POSITIVE, what's the chance you're actually sick?
column6:
A) About 99%
B) About 50%
C) About 10%
D) About 1%
E) Do not know
column9: Only about 10%! Out of 1,000 people: 1 is sick (tests positive), 999 aren't (but ~10 falsely test positive). So ~11 positives total, only 1 truly sick = ~9%. Rare diseases produce many false positives. That's why doctors order follow-up tests.
column11: Risk numeracy / risk literacy item bank.

column4: What is the approximate probability that at least one member of a 65-year-old couple today will live to age 90 or beyond?

A) Less than 25%
B) About 25-40%
C) About 50-60%
D) More than 60%
E) Do not know
column9: About 50-60%! People underestimate how long they'll live. For a couple, you only need ONE to reach 90. Even if each has a 40% individual chance, the combined probability is much higher. Plan for 25-30+ years of retirement!
